abstract: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for deployment. A controller at the model–tool boundary reuses resolved decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal arguments, causal dependencies and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions, unsupported evidence and selector abstention invoke the original actor again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43% to 85.71% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52% lower cost than retained callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.

sections.body: The introduction describes the problem: after each tool result, a harness decides whether to reason again or execute an action that earlier reasoning already resolved. It introduces HarnessMM, which keeps model weights, tools and task interfaces fixed. A controller stores resolved decisions as Executable Decision Graphs, checks them with Guarded Decision Reuse and runs them through Certified Callback Substitution. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refines companion harness configurations, and validation selects the one deployed. On 98 HumanEval test tasks, Codex keeps 90.82% success while Tokens/task (k) fall from 66.72 to 47.02. The authors note that selection, authorship and fallback costs can offset the savings.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Harnesses re-invoke reasoning after each tool result, even when earlier reasoning already fixed the next action.

sections.body: The related-work section sorts prior work into four strands. Prompt, context and reasoning compression reduce the size or depth of a call. Fast–slow agents and model routing change which model reasons and how deeply. Skills, memory and reusable programs can inform future reasoning or encapsulate a routine. Agent and harness optimization improves prompts and configurations from feedback. The authors contrast these with an Executable Decision Graph, which stores episode-specific, fully resolved commitments that can replace a reasoning call. They also note that Jev motivates typed compact decisions, but a selector alone does not establish callback elimination.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior methods reduce, route or reuse calls, while HarnessMM targets whether a future reasoning call must recur.

sections.body: The formulation treats the actor parameters as fixed and asks for the lowest expected token cost of a policy, subject to a bound on capability regret against the original harness for each declared benchmark. Each node in a computation graph contributes its model-token cost when invoked. The authors define the Substitution Paradox: a fast stage that removes none of an original continuation's tokens adds its own cost, so typed output or frequent fast-path use does not by itself establish savings. A beneficial substitution requires that removed computation exceed introduced computation, where introduced computation includes authorship, routing, added context and any fallback or recovery. The cost condition and the quality constraint address separate requirements.
sections.heading: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Substitution saves cost only when removed reasoning tokens exceed the tokens introduced by authorship, routing and fallback.

sections.body: The method stores each resolved decision as a node in an Executable Decision Graph, holding a native action, its complete literal arguments, a predecessor and a public guard. A node is eligible when its predecessor has completed, its guard holds on observed receipts and its arguments are closed. A unique eligible node executes deterministically, while an empty set or an abstention invokes the original actor. Certified Callback Substitution runs the exact action through the native interface and issues a certificate binding the graph hash, the decision identifier, the predecessor receipt, the executed arguments, the tool receipt and the bypassed callback identifier. The authors state the limit: a passing guard proves only its declared public condition, and whether earlier reasoning correctly resolved the action is a semantic assumption assessed through task scoring.
sections.heading: HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions
sections.headline: Guarded reuse executes stored actions only when public guards hold, and otherwise returns control to the original actor.

sections.body: Table 1 reports paired HumanEval results on 98 test tasks. Codex keeps 90.82% success while Tokens/task (k) fall from 66.72 to 47.02. DeepSeek Harness rises from 71.43% to 85.71% success, and its paid model calls fall from 954 to 415. On the 257 MBPP-sanitized tasks, the ablation gives full HarnessMM 93.77% success at 13.17 Tokens/task (k), against 18.03 without graph reuse and 16.37 with retained callbacks. The authors state that integrated harness effects combine reuse, context management and finalization, so the ablation alone isolates persistence and callback removal. Companion studies on other benchmarks are reported separately. The DeepSeek paired outcomes give a two-sided exact McNemar p of 0.0161.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On 98 HumanEval test tasks, HarnessMM keeps Codex success at 90.82% and raises DeepSeek Harness success to 85.71%.

sections.body: The limitations section names several conditions on the savings. They depend on provider input, cache and context accounting, and on whether resolved actions are available at a given boundary. New semantic decisions still require slow reasoning. Authorship, selection and recovery can outweigh the calls avoided. Public-state adapters are task specific, and the integration does not assume arbitrary task semantics can be inferred automatically. Small development sets leave policy-level quality differences uncertain.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Savings depend on provider accounting and resolved-action availability, and adapters are task specific.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the method: HarnessMM stores resolved decisions, checks when they can execute, and uses them to replace repeated reasoning calls. On all 98 HumanEval test tasks, it preserves Codex success at 90.82% with 29.54% fewer actor tokens. It improves DeepSeek Harness from 71.43% to 85.71% with 87.93% fewer tokens. The MBPP ablation isolates persistence and callback removal. The companion studies keep their own configuration scope.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Stored, guard-checked decisions can replace repeated reasoning calls, and companion studies keep their own scope.

sections.body: Appendix A gives Table 2, paired success, Tokens/task (k) and Calls/task for eight RSI iterations on 32 MiniWoB++ training tasks per arm, comparing single-use graphs with HarnessMM. It states that the curve measures candidate execution efficiency, not autonomous optimizer rounds or held-out tests. Appendix B records the QA profile and rule-development protocols; four arms with identical final request bytes each solve 78.91% of tasks at 3.02 Tokens/task (k). Appendix C documents the native adapter, guards and bank audits. The appendix also reports the MBPP DeepSeek Harness comparison, where it notes that the 40% target against both baselines remains open.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives per-iteration MiniWoB++ RSI measurements, development protocols, implementation details and paired-effect definitions.
